title: Give with faith, give with fear
hookLine: an old send-off for graduating students says give with fear. why fear?
carry: dana: the manner travels with the gift
tomorrow: count every can, or stop counting? one book, two answers.

cards: A graduation speech can sound like a greeting card: follow your dreams, be kind, call home. An old one, in the Taittiriya Upanishad, has a teacher sending off students who've finished their study.
Speak the truth, he says. Follow dharma. Honor your mother and father.
Then a short list on giving, and one line in it sounds wrong. Give with fear. Not with joy, not with love.
Fear. Why would a teacher send students off with that?

teach.b: Here's the whole list, in paraphrase. Give with faith, and don't give without it. Give from your plenty.
Give with modesty. Give with fear. Give with understanding.
The Sanskrit for the odd line is bhiya, with fear, and readers hear it more than one way. Some hear awe: the giver stands a little in awe of what giving is.

teach.h: BHIYA: AWE, OR WORRY IT'S TOO SMALL.
teach.b: Some hear a worry that the gift is too small, or will be given badly. Either way, look at the line beside it. Hriya, with modesty, even a little shyness.
Neither word is about the size of the gift. Both are about the giver: not puffed up, not careless.

teach.h: THE GITA'S THREE KINDS OF GIFT.
teach.b: The Gita takes the question further, in chapter seventeen, sorting gifts into three kinds. The clear kind is given because giving is right, to someone who can't pay it back, at a fitting place and time.
The restless kind is given expecting a return, or grudgingly, with a wince. The dark kind goes to the wrong place, at the wrong time, without respect, even with contempt.
All three are gifts; something changes hands every time. But a gift carries more than the thing. Contempt rides along.
So does a hidden invoice. So does respect. That's the puzzle, close to solved: the fear is the opposite of swagger.

teach.h: DANA: THE MANNER TRAVELS WITH THE GIFT.
teach.b: Hindus have a name for giving, dana, and this is how it's taught: the manner travels with the gift. And it's the third design rule for a year of service.

teach.h: PLAN THE MANNER, NOT JUST THE AMOUNT.
teach.b: Plan the manner, not just the amount.

how: Hindu teachers draw on the Taittiriya send-off and the Gita's three kinds of gift when they speak about dana, giving: how to give, not only how much.

o: action done with modesty, so a gift keeps respect
a reward that comes back to the giver in kind
a debt that grows each time someone gives too little

games.q: the manner of giving — tap the pairs.
p: with fear: awe, or worry it's too small

s: in the Gita's sorting, the bigger the gift, the better
the Gita sorts gifts by how they're given: to whom, when, and with what respect, not by size.
the teacher's send-off includes the line give with fear
bhiya: readers hear awe, or a worry that the gift is too small.
a gift given with contempt doesn't count as a gift at all
it's still a gift; the Gita calls it the dark kind.

games.q: your cousin wants to pay for a friend's lunch when money's tight for them, and plans to announce it at the table 'so it's not awkward.' by the teacher's list, what's better?
o: announce it. being open about it is honest.
pay quietly, so the gift asks nothing back.
skip it. it might embarrass them either way.
games.why: give with modesty, the teacher says; the Gita's clear gift goes to someone who can't repay, with respect. an announcement can turn a gift into a show.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms open and turned up, the way someone holds out a gift. Keep them there through the sit. Bring to mind one gift you could give with nobody watching, and let your open hands hold it quietly.

wordCard.voice: Karma, in the giving, what Hindus call dana: with faith, with modesty, with a little awe, so the gift carries respect and no invoice.

orig.note: Sanskrit: give with fear, one line of the teacher's send-off in Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.

carryVoice: For the road: dana, giving the Hindu way, where the manner travels with the gift. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.1–3 (the teacher's parting instruction to students: speak truth, follow dharma, honor mother and father; give with faith, not without faith, from plenty, with modesty, with fear, with understanding)
Bhagavad Gita 17.20–22 (the three kinds of gift: sattvic, rajasic, tamasic)
